turn_text: So I'm here with Justin Amash, Congressman from Michigan's their district. So super exciting news to this week. You're now you're running for president. I think, you know, people have been talking about this for a while, but tell us why you decided to run.

Well, you look at the candidates and they're not exactly impressive. You've got two candidates that aren't appealing to most Americans. And I think people deserve a choice. They deserve a choice that's different from what the two parties are offering right now in Washington. And even when you look at this COVID-19 situation with the type of responses we've seen, we've seen the parties offering basically the same thing. you know, they formulate it slightly differently, but for the most part, they're giving you the same kind of COVID-19 response, which is a big convoluted program, getting the government involved in everything, centrally planning the economy. And I think there are obvious libertarian answers to the way we might address this, and there are obvious libertarian answers to the way we might address a lot of things that are much more appealing to a broad segment of the population.

Why did you give some examples of that? Because what would you do differently? I mean, how would a policy standpoint from your presidency be different than what's gone on with the Trump presidency, let's say just last year or so?

There may be a lot of differences over the last year. When you're looking at the COVID-19 response, the answer is obvious. I mean, he pushed for a big, convoluted program with much of the money going to Wall Street, to big banks, And even when it comes to small businesses, a lot of the relief was put in the hands of banks and other people. And really those who have the best connections are the ones getting the relief from the government. And regular people are being left out in the cold. And I had suggested to the extent you are going to do something, you might as well get the money to the people. And that would mean some kind of emergency UBI of sorts, getting paychecks in people's hands as quickly as possible and having that go for the duration of the crisis. And then when it comes to how you handle the states, he's sent mixed messages the whole time. One day he wants to be a king of the country telling everyone exactly what to do. Really what you need is a steady leader, someone who's going to bring confidence, have the respect of governors across the country and have the respect of the public. turn_text: Can you give us a quick story about some example, you're talking about the mob bosses within the party. And can you give an example, some of you experienced that you could disclose, maybe, I don't know if you could give names or not, but just to give people a flavor of, I guess, the dysfunctional nature of the parties and the ability for a representative who might be a really good person or have come in with the best of intentions, and they're incapable of voting the way they want because of other things that they can't control.

Yeah. Well, I mean, just as a general matter over the years, individual members of Congress have had less and less power. And that's also true of committees. It used to be true that committees could actually influence the system a lot more than they do. And these days, committees are almost neutered. I mean, you have the speaker of the house controlling the thing and Republican and Democratic leaders control the entire process from the top down. And members of Congress come in thinking they can change things. And I certainly thought I could change a lot of things too from the inside. And I realized that actually it was practically impossible unless you were willing to vent to the will of the leadership team. And as soon as you vent to their will, you weren't really fighting for what you intended to fight for anyways. So you weren't doing the things you were supposed to do. So I've seen so many members of Congress come in and they all come in with the good intentions. They want to limit government or do whatever it might be that the voters elected them to do. And then they get there and they're told, well, if you wanted to do this, then we'll need you to, if you want to get on the committee you want to get on or if you want to get your legislation on the floor, you'll need to do this thing for us. And that thing will be voting for something bad. And then they'll vote for it. And then they'll get some kind of token reward that is minor compared to the kind of destruction they're doing. And then, you know, weeks later, they'll say, Oh, well, we want you to do this additional bad thing. It's a little bit worse than the previous one, but not that much worse. And, and just, you know, do one, do it for the team, take one for the team where we have to fight the other side and the other side is evil. And that's how they'll always present it. And then you say, well, I guess, what am I going to do? People say, the other side is evil. So I guess I have to make the most of it and just go with its team again. And these members do it for a few months. And you look six months later and you can't even recognize the person. It's like their soul has been sucked out of them. They're a totally different entity now. And this happens time and again. people have to sell their souls, essentially, to get anything moving. And that's a really disgusting part of the system. And I refuse to play along. I would fight the leadership on all sorts of things. And the times we would get our way where we get some opening of the system, where we'd be able to push things further, was when we had the House Freedom Caucus actually caring about the process. That was a brief period of time where the House Freedom Caucus really cared about opening up the process and getting amendments on the floor and doing other things that were necessary. And we were quite effective for a brief period of time until the president came along and now the House Freedom Caucus, largely just cheerleaders for the president, which is unfortunate, but not unexpected.
